Since you are targeting an academic paper, you need to frame this problem using precise, formal operations research and networking terminology. In academic literature, your architecture is classified as a Time-Varying Topology (TVT) Virtual Topology Design and Call Admission Control (CAC) problem.
To structure your paper effectively, here is the exact theoretical framing, mathematical formulation, and a high-level literature roadmap you will need.
1. Formal Problem Definition & Classifications
In the abstract and methodology sections of your paper, you should classify the problem using these established domain concepts:
• Time-Sliced Space-Time Graph: Because you discretize the continuous orbit into 5-minute increments, your network is modeled as a sequence of static snapshot graphs \(G_t = (V_t, E_t)\).
• Restricted Route Multi-Commodity Flow (RR-MCF): A traditional Multi-Commodity Flow (MCF) problem allows traffic to split across any arbitrary paths. Because your hardware restricts routing to exactly two pre-configured interfaces (Primary and Secondary), you must explicitly define this as a Restricted Route or Path-Constrained MCF.
• Non-Preemptive Priority Call Admission Control: Your absolute priority rules mean that higher-tier traffic cannot be degraded by lower-tier traffic, and your "all-or-nothing" constraint makes it a binary admission problem rather than a continuous flow problem.
2. The Formal Mathematical Formulation (MILP)
Academic papers require a formal optimization model, even if you ultimately implement a heuristic to solve it. Here is the Mixed-Integer Linear Program (MILP) formulation for a single 5-minute snapshot \(t\), isolated to a single priority tier \(P\).
Sets and Parameters:
• \(K_{P}\): The set of active communication requests (commodities) belonging to priority tier \(P\).
• \(E\): The set of active directed links (Optical Crosslinks + RF Uplinks/Downlinks) in the current snapshot.
• \(C_{e}\): The residual bandwidth capacity of link \(e \in E\) (after higher priority tiers have been routed).
• \(d_{k}\): The hard bandwidth demand requested by mobile terminal \(k \in K_P\).
• \(L_{k,1}, L_{k,2}\): The end-to-end latency of the Primary and Secondary paths for request \(k\).
• \(S_k \in \{0, 1\}\): A parameter indicating if the primary path of request \(k\) utilizes the same first-hop satellite as the previous time slice (1 if sticky, 0 if roaming).
Decision Variables:
• \(x_{k,1} \in \{0, 1\}\): 1 if request \(k\) is accepted on its Primary path; 0 otherwise.
• \(x_{k,2} \in \{0, 1\}\): 1 if request \(k\) is accepted on its Secondary path; 0 otherwise.
Objective Function:
To minimize latency while maximizing admission under absolute priorities, you use a lexicographic weight approach:
\(\text{Maximize\ }\sum _{k\in K_{P}}\mathbf{M}\cdot (x_{k,1}+x_{k,2})-\sum _{k\in K_{P}}\left(L_{k,1}\cdot x_{k,1}+L_{k,2}\cdot x_{k,2}\right)+\sum _{k\in K_{P}}\mathbf{\gamma }\cdot S_{k}\cdot x_{k,1}\)
• \(\mathbf{M}\): A dominant scale factor (\(\mathbf{M} \gg L\)) enforcing throughput maximization first.
• \(\mathbf{\gamma }\): A tuning parameter that rewards the system for maintaining a "sticky" first hop.
Constraints:
1. All-or-Nothing Path Selection: A request can use at most one path, and cannot be fractionally split.
\(x_{k,1}+x_{k,2}\le 1\quad \forall k\in K_{P}\)
2. Strict Residual Link Capacity: The aggregate traffic admitted across all paths using link \(e\) cannot exceed its residual capacity.
\(\sum _{k\in K_{P}}d_{k}\cdot \left(\delta _{k,1}^{e}\cdot x_{k,1}+\delta _{k,2}^{e}\cdot x_{k,2}\right)\le C_{e}\quad \forall e\in E\)
(Where \(\delta_{k,p}^e = 1\) if path \(p\) of request \(k\) traverses link \(e\), and 0 otherwise).
3. Key Academic Literature to Cite
To anchor your paper, look up and cite papers covering these specific paradigms:
• Predictive Space-Time Graph Models: Read papers by H. Chang et al. on "Topological Design and Routing in Mega-Constellations." They pioneered the concept of discretizing LEO orbits into predictable, periodic graph snapshots.
• Max-Min Fairness in Constrained Networks: Look into Bertsekas and Gallager's foundational work on data networks for how to mathematically prove your tie-breaking/gap-splitting rule.
• Greedy Heuristics vs. LP Relaxations: Cite literature comparing MILP performance bounds to greedy sorting algorithms (specifically Greedy Randomized Adaptive Search Procedures - GRASP) in satellite network admission control.
4. Structuring Your Paper's "Contributions" Section
In academic peer reviews, your paper will be judged heavily on its clear articulation of novelty. You should position your core contributions as:
1. Enforcing Static Routing Layouts via 2-Path Confinement: Most academic papers assume satellites can dynamically recalculate routing matrices on the fly. Your paper provides a realistic constraint by forcing the optimization to choose strictly between a pre-configured Primary and Secondary path.
2. Multi-Objective Heuristic for High-Density admission: Proposing the multi-key sorting strategy (Priority \(\rightarrow \) Stickiness \(\rightarrow \) First-Hop Load \(\rightarrow \) Latency) proves that a low-complexity algorithm can mimic an NP-Hard MILP solver within the tight 5-minute operational windows of massive LEO constellations.
